SYNTHETIC TEST MATERIAL
PSY 101: Introduction to Psychology, Fall 2026
Instructor: Dr. Marcus Hallowell, Brandt Hall 214, mhallowell@example.edu
Office hours: Tue/Thu 1:00-2:30 pm, or by appointment

COURSE DESCRIPTION
This course surveys the major areas of psychology: research methods, the brain and behavior, perception, learning, memory, development, personality, psychological disorders, and treatment. Students practice reading research critically and applying concepts to everyday life.

WEEKLY SCHEDULE (weeks begin Monday)
Week 1 (Aug 24): What is psychology? History and perspectives
Week 2 (Aug 31): Research methods and ethics
Week 3 (Sep 7): Biological bases of behavior (no class Mon Sep 7, Labor Day)
Week 4 (Sep 14): Sensation and perception
Week 5 (Sep 21): Consciousness and sleep
Week 6 (Sep 28): Classical and operant conditioning
Week 7 (Oct 5): Observational learning, review of learning
Week 8 (Oct 12): Midterm review; MIDTERM EXAM Thu Oct 15
Week 9 (Oct 19): Memory: encoding, storage, retrieval, forgetting
Week 10 (Oct 26): Thinking, language, intelligence
Week 11 (Nov 2): Lifespan development
Week 12 (Nov 9): Motivation and emotion
Week 13 (Nov 16): Personality
Week 14 (Nov 23): Stress and health (no class Thu Nov 26, Thanksgiving)
Week 15 (Nov 30): Psychological disorders
Week 16 (Dec 7): Treatment of disorders, final review
Final exam week: Dec 14-18

QUIZZES (online, open Fri 8:00 am, due Sat 11:59 pm, 20 questions, 30 minutes)
Quiz 1: Sat Sep 12, research methods and ethics
Quiz 2: Sat Sep 26, biological bases and sensation/perception
Quiz 3: Sat Oct 10, conditioning and learning
Quiz 4: Sat Oct 24, memory (encoding, storage, retrieval, forgetting)
Quiz 5: Sat Nov 14, thinking, intelligence, and development
Quiz 6: Sat Dec 5, personality, stress, and disorders
Your lowest quiz score is dropped.

EXAMS
Midterm Exam: Thu Oct 15, in class, covers Weeks 1-7. Multiple choice and short answer.
Final Exam: Tue Dec 15, 10:30 am-12:30 pm, Brandt Hall 120. Cumulative, with extra emphasis on Weeks 9-16.

GRADING BREAKDOWN
Quizzes (best 5 of 6): 20%
Midterm Exam: 25%
Final Exam: 30%
Research participation or article summaries: 10%
Reading responses and in-class activities: 10%
Attendance and participation: 5%
Grades: A 93+, A- 90, B+ 87, B 83, B- 80, C+ 77, C 73, C- 70, D 60-69, F below 60.

POLICIES
1. Late work: Reading responses lose 10% per day late and are not accepted after 5 days. Quizzes close at the posted deadline; missed quizzes count as the dropped quiz.
2. Make-up exams: Make-up exams are given only for documented illness or emergencies. Contact the instructor before the exam when possible.
3. Academic integrity: All exams and quizzes are individual work. Using AI tools or notes not permitted by the instructor is a violation and will be reported to the Dean of Students.

The instructor may adjust dates with advance notice posted on the course site and announced in class.
notes:
PSY 101 notes - Emily

TOPIC 1: CLASSICAL CONDITIONING (Pavlov)
- learning thru association, 2 stimuli get paired
- UCS (food) -> UCR (salivation), natural, no learning needed
- NS (bell) + UCS repeated -> bell becomes CS -> CR (salivate to bell alone)
- acquisition = CS & UCS paired; timing matters, CS shd come just BEFORE UCS (~0.5 sec best)
- extinction = CS w/o UCS over & over, CR fades
- spontaneous recovery = CR comes back after rest period (!! ext. isn't total erasing)
- generalization = similar stimuli trigger CR (Little Albert + white rabbit)
- discrimination = only respond to the specific CS
- Little Albert (Watson) = fear cond. of rat, unethical, prof said never repeat today
- real life ex: nausea at smell of food that once made me sick (taste aversion), 1 trial learning, Garcia
- NOT same as operant!! classical = involuntary resp, operant = voluntary behavior + consequences

TOPIC 2: MEMORY (Atkinson-Shiffrin)
- 3 stages: sensory memory -> STM/working memory -> LTM
- sensory: v. brief (iconic ~ 0.5 sec, echoic ~ 3-4 sec)
- STM: ~7 +/- 2 items (Miller), ~20-30 sec w/o rehearsal; chunking helps (phone #s)
- maintenance rehearsal = repeat; elaborative rehearsal = connect to meaning -> better for LTM
- LTM: explicit (declarative) = episodic (events) + semantic (facts); implicit (nondeclarative) = procedural (riding bike), priming
- encoding -> storage -> retrieval
- retrieval cues, context-dependent memory (study where u test?), state-dependent
- serial position effect: primacy + recency, middle items forgotten
- Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: steep drop first hrs/days, then levels off
- spacing effect > cramming (ugh)
- TODO: reread ch. 8 on false memories (Loftus) before quiz 4, make flashcards for episodic vs semantic
